newsitem.title: UK: Physical sugar - EU premiums seen steady into 1997.
newsitem.headline: Physical sugar - EU premiums seen steady into 1997.

text.p: Premiums for European Union (EU) white sugar should hold steady into 1997 despite ample supply as an influx of Polish sugars reduces the market's overall deliverable quality, physical brokers said on Thursday.

December is traditionally a period of good EU supply but the arrival of lesser-quality 60 ICUMSA cargoes on the scene -- the last two futures expiries both saw Polish deliveries -- had the effect of increasing demand for quality EU cargoes, they said.
"It is trading flattish and there's going to be a small premium," said one trader, referring to next year's EU cargoes.
"It's not going to go to a discount but I don't think you're going to see an improvement in these small premiums. I wouldn't be surprised to see it flat a lot of the time," a broker said.
Polish sugar just qualifies as deliverable under the terms of the No.5 contract but the bulk of the terminal market's supply comes from the EU, which produces a higher quality.
"There will always be the fear that Polish sugar will be delivered and so the basis of the No.5 now is taking delivery of Polish sugar," said
Traders quoted EU premiums at $5 over March for shipment in December/January but said prices were nominal and Antwerp cargoes, as usual, would command higher prices.

Antwerp premiums were quoted at $10 last traded for the same period and bid/offered at $4/8 for January/February. Minor delays at European ports have also kept cash prices supported. "The ports are quite busy in Europe for December and with the weather not being so good, some shipments are a bit delayed," said a physical broker.

"The ports are practically full but it's more or less...on schedule with about 15 days delay," he said. But EU premiums should not rise too far due to the ample supply and increased competition from Middle East refineries. India's offers of cheap lower-quality cargoes have also displaced some traditional homes for EU sugars.

As many players had priced cargoes forward, a buying vacuum could ensue with little demand seen in the spot physical market which would lead to a further weakening in prices, brokers said. "You've got two huge refineries coming up in the Middle East churning out sugar and the Indians have filled in places where perhaps traditional EU quality sugar would go," said another broker.
"They've managed to impress people into buying low-quality whites because they're offering it so cheap -- so suddenly homes are disappearing."
Physical offtake has recently been scarce although Tunisia made a pre-Ramadan purchase on Wednesday and bought a 45 ICUMSA cargo at $328.75 per tonne from a major London trade house.

But although the spot value of the No.5 contract currently stands at the lowest level since February 1994, buyers have been reluctant to emerge and key players on the demand side such as Russia have still to make their requirements clear.
"There may be a few buyers holding off...Russia is still putting things off, they haven't really come to the market," the trader said.
"I think the market has got to go lower before we see some serious offtake," said one futures trader, citing 10.20 cents/lb basis New York's March raws contract as a key support level.
